newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia announces heavy cut to 1997/98 immigration.
newsitem.headline: Australia announces heavy cut to 1997/98 immigration.

text.p: Australia on Wednesday heavily cut its annual immigration intake for the second consecutive year, citing concerns over stubbornly high unemployment.

Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock said the number of migrants allowed into the country in the year from July would be cut more than eight percent to 68,000 from 74,000 in 1996/97, with a shift in focus to work skills instead of family reunion.
"The government believes that because of high levels of unemployment, a further reduction in migration is desirable at this time," Ruddock said.
Ruddock denied the government was bowing to pressure from race row Pauline Hanson, who has demanded an immediate ban on migrants to help combat Australia's chronic unemployment.
"... this is not a response to the comments of Pauline Hanson. If it were a response to Pauline Hanson there would probably be no programme at all," he told reporters.
Voters have flocked to Hanson's newly-formed One Nation Party, which leading opinion polls now rank as potentially the third force in politics, ahead of the Australian Democrats.
Australia's jobless rate has remained stuck above 8.5 percent for more than a year and the government has forecast little improvement over the next year.

Prime Minister John Howard, who sparked a race row in 1988 when he criticised high Asian immigration levels, quickly cut migrant numbers just months after winning office in March 1996, announcing an 11 percent reduction for 1996/97.
Under Howard's administration, the proportion of migrants allowed in for their work skills has jumped to more than half from one third in the last year of the former Labor government.
Family reunion numbers -- which have favoured Asian migrants in recent years -- will fall to 47 percent of the total in 1997/98 from almost 70 percent in 1995/96.
"The government has further strengthened the emphasis on the skilled intake, while maintaining a commitment to bona fide immediate family migrants," Ruddock said.
Places for asylum seekers has been maintained at 12,000.
But despite substantial cuts to its annual immigration intake, Australia continues to take a high number of migrants in proportion to its 18 million population.
